profile.summary: Hosea presents, through the marital pain of the prophet, a living image of the pain of God before the unfaithfulness of his people. The book is born in a period of severe instability in the northern kingdom: unequal prosperity, violent succession of kings, foreign threat, and ultimately the fall of Israel in 722 BC. In this scenario, the prophet announces royal and imminent judgment, but also insists that the God of the covenant not abandon his people. Divine justice is severe because sin is serious; yet God's mercy seeks to restore his chosen ones. The central message is that the Lord disciplines to redeem, and not just to condemn.
profile.setting: The ministry of Hosea develops in the kingdom of northern Israel, approximately between 760 BC and just before the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. The scenario is of great political and spiritual turmoil: at the end of the reign of Jeroboam II there was territorial expansion and wealth for some, but also poverty for many. After his death, the kingdom went through rapid instability, with several kings in a few years and successive murders. At the same time, foreign powers threatened the country. Instead of turning to the Lord, Israel was further in idolatry, which would culminate in destruction by Assyria. As for the formation of the book, the tradition presented suggests that Oseias preached orally and that his oracles were later gathered by him or his followers; the final wording may have occurred in Judah after the fall of the north.

structure.label: The marriage of Hosea and the prophetic sign
structure.description: The first chapters describe the prophet's painful experience with his unfaithful wife, not as a simple biography, but as a sign of the wounded relationship between the Lord and Israel. The judgment is announced, but the hope of restoration already appears.

structure.label: Accusations against Israel
structure.description: From here, the book brings together prophetic denunciations against the people and, in a special way, against their leaderships. The infidelity of the nation is exposed as a breaking of the covenant and rejection of the Lord.

structure.label: Imminent judgment and promise of restoration
structure.description: Prophecies advance in a tone of increasing crisis, with national destruction in sight. Still, the book ends with the reaffirmation that God will not give up his people and promises to restore it.

themes: The covenant between the Lord and Israel
Divine judgment as a form of discipline
Mercy and restoration after the fall
readingKeys: Notice how the marriage of Hosea acts as an image of the relationship between God and Israel, without reducing the book to mere personal narrative.
Notice the constant tension between denunciation and hope: judgment is real, but it is never the last word.
Note the emphasis on Israel's leadership and the historical context of crisis, as this helps to understand the urgency of warnings.
profile.cautions: The introduction does not provide enough detail to reconstruct each episode of the book, so you'll be sure to avoid overly speculative readings about Hosea's personal life. The authorship and final essay are presented with some caution: it is known of the ministry of the prophet, but the final form of the book may have been organized later, possibly in Judah. The evangelical reader must also realize that divine mercy in Hosea does not eliminate judgment, but crosses it with the aim of restoring the unfaithful people.

dossier.narratedEra: The book narrates the ministry of Hosea in the kingdom of Northern Israel, especially between the end of Jeroboam II's long reign and the fall of Israel to Assyria in the 8th century BC; the notes also place action in a period of great political instability in the last decades of the kingdom.
dossier.compositionEra: The notes indicate that the prophecies were proclaimed throughout about 760 BC until just before 722 BC; the final wording is presented as possibly occurring after the fall of Israel, perhaps in Judah, when Hosea or his followers gathered the oracles in an anthology. Matthew Henry also considers him the first of the prophets writers, prior to Isaiah, and the ancient tradition associates him with Beth-Semes and the tribe of Issachar, although this is only tradition cited in the introduction.

politics.title: End of Jeroboam II's reign and unequal prosperity
politics.detail: Hosea began his ministry in the northern kingdom at the end of Jeroboam II's long and stable reign. The note points out that although Jeroboam was a bad king, he was strong enough to expand Israel's borders. This expansion generated wealth for some, but impoverished others.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of Hosea gains strong social contrast: the apparent national force did not mean fidelity to God, and external prosperity hid internal injustice and spiritual vulnerability.
politics.reference: The 1:1; context of 2 Rs 14:23-28 according to the introductory note.

politics.title: Successive strikes in the Northern Kingdom
politics.detail: In the last three decades of the Northern kingdom, six kings occupied the throne of Israel; only one died of natural death and four were murdered. The note in Oseias 7 describes this period as bloody political intrigue and violent succession.
politics.readingImpact: This causes accusations against leaders and conspiracies in Hoemes 7 to be read in response to a real institutional collapse, not as religious abstractions.

politics.title: Assyria as a decisive threat
politics.detail: The introduction states that hostile foreign powers threatened to destroy the nation and that the Assyrian empire destroyed the Northern kingdom in 722 BC. The notes of Hoeas 7 also describe the Assyrian invasion as a factor that led Israel to react with political despair.
politics.readingImpact: The judgment of Hosea ceases to appear generic: he speaks to a nation in geopolitical agony, trying to survive by human means while rejecting the Lord.
politics.reference: The 7:7, 7:11; fall of Israel in 722 BC according to the introduction.

politics.title: Assyria and Egypt as rival diplomatic poles
politics.detail: Hosea 7 presents Israel frantically oscillating between Assyria and Egypt, seeking treaties and alliances to escape destruction. The note states that the people have ignored the Lord both in international and internal politics.
politics.readingImpact: Prophetic criticism is understood as a denunciation of faithless diplomacy: external alliances do not replace dependence on God.

politics.title: Disunity between Israel and Judah
politics.detail: The note of Hosea 1:11 notes that for nearly 200 years Israel and Judah were divided by political rivalry; the promised restoration would gather the two under one leader, as in the days of David.
politics.readingImpact: The final promise is not only spiritual, but also political and national: the future of God includes reunification and reversal of exile.

customs.title: Marriage as a prophetic sign and domestic drama
customs.detail: Chapters 1-3 are presented as the clipping of the prophet's life with his unfaithful wife, Gomer. The notes say that the goal is not biography, but to illustrate God's painful relationship with Israel.
customs.readingImpact: The prophet's family experience functions as a lens to interpret the covenant: domestic adultery clarifies the gravity of Israel's spiritual infidelity.

customs.title: Debate on the condition of Gomer
customs.detail: The note records that many ancient interpreters understood the account symbolically; today, most consider the marriage real, but differs about Gômer's past: a common prostitute, a cultual prostitute or a woman still not practicing immorality, although predisposed to it.
customs.readingImpact: The reader is instructed to recognize that the note does not fix all the historical details of the prophet's house; the focus is on the theological function of marriage.

customs.title: Children with prophetic names
customs.detail: The names of the sons of Hosea are presented as part of the prophetic message. Lo-Ruama and Lo-Ami communicate judgment; then, the same names are reversed for hope and restoration.
customs.readingImpact: Family life becomes public language. The reader should hear in the names a preaching staggered about judgment and reversal of luck.

customs.title: Domestic economy and husband provision
customs.detail: The introduction describes the Lord as a loving husband, as the one who provided Israel with land, food, drink, clothing, and safety. In Oseias 14, restoration is described with fertility and nutrition images, such as refreshing dew and deep roots.
customs.readingImpact: Metaphors show that the covenant includes material sustenance, not only religious devotion; Israel's infidelity appears as ingratitude for concrete goods.
customs.reference: The 14:5-7; thematic panorama of the introduction.

customs.title: Singing-beliecist and body practices
customs.detail: The notes speak of Israel using Canaan gods, including forms linked to fertility, and mention self-mutilation as a characteristic of the Canaanite cult, forbidden in Israel. In Hosea 14, the people are urged to abandon foreign idols and alliances.
customs.readingImpact: The popular cult is not treated as neutral or merely diverse; it is seen as marital infidelity and betrayal of the covenant.

language.title: Marriage language for the alliance
language.detail: The introduction insists that marriage is a powerful symbol of the covenant relationship between the Lord and his people. Israel is described as an adulterous wife; God, as an offended husband and desirous of rescuing the unfaithful wife.
language.readingImpact: This resource controls the reading of the book: sin is not only legal disobedience, but also peaceful adultery against the covenant's own husband.
language.reference: The 1-3; also 14:1-4 in the logic of the restoration.

language.title: Symbolic names and reversal of meaning
language.detail: Jezreel, Lo-Ruama, and Lo-Ami are treated as names preaching judgment. Then Hosea transforms the names of the children into signs of blessing and hope; Jezreel comes to signify growth and not just judgment.
language.readingImpact: The reader needs to realize that the text operates for exchange of meanings: what marked sentence can be reconfigured by sovereign action of God.

language.title: Agricultural and climatic images
language.detail: Hosea 14 uses dew, roots, cedars from Lebanon and shadow to describe the healing and stability that God would give to Israel. The note highlights dew as a vital source in semi-desertic climate.
language.readingImpact: The restoration is realized by images of daily living and real environment; the reader understands that the promised grace is as tangible as moisture, growth and shelter.

language.title: Metaphors of decomposition, fraud and uselessness
language.detail: In Hosea 7, Israel is compared to a badly baked cake, to a dove without judgment, to a loose bow and to a bird trapped by trap. The note also draws attention to the hunter's net as a figure of divine judgment.
language.readingImpact: The images make the foolishness and the national impotence palpable. Instead of political force, Israel appears as something broken, incomplete and unable to reach the target.

language.title: Vocabulary of healing, redemption and grief
language.detail: The note in Hosea 7 notes that sad what is a funeral word, suggesting that Israel is as dead in the eyes of God. He also explains how to pay a price to repatriate someone enslaved, associated with the exodus.
language.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the book alternates lament and hope with technical rescue vocabulary: the God who thinks he also desires to repurchase and restore.

timeline.title: Ministry of Hosea between about 760 and 722 BC.
timeline.detail: The introduction places the prophet's ministry in the Northern kingdom from about 760 BC until shortly before the fall of Israel in 722 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: Oracles are read as prolonged speech to a real historical crisis, not as a collection of words without temporal context.

timeline.title: Last years of Jeroboam II's reign
timeline.detail: Hosea began prophesizing at the end of Jeroboam II's reign, which lasted from 793 to 753 BC, a period of relative stability before collapse.
timeline.readingImpact: The prophetic message is still born under apparent national prosperity, which reinforces the contrast between political success and spiritual ruin.

timeline.title: Fall of Jezreel under Tiglath-Pileser III in 733 BC.
timeline.detail: The note of Hosea 1:5 states that Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria fulfilled the prophecy in 733 BC, defeating Israeli forces and capturing the valley of Jezreel.
timeline.readingImpact: Prophecy is read as a verifiable historical anticipation within the note itself, reinforcing the concrete character of the judgment announced.

timeline.title: Final period with seven kings and internal violence
timeline.detail: Hosea 7:3-7 is situated at the end of twenty-five years of the kingdom of the North, when seven kings followed and four were murdered by usurpers.
timeline.readingImpact: The prophetic accusations against deception, conspiracy and regicide are read in the scenario of accelerated state disintegration.

timeline.title: Destruction of Israel in 722 BC
timeline.detail: The introduction states that the Assyrian empire destroyed the Northern kingdom in 722 BC. The book then ends with promise of restoration after the catastrophe.
timeline.readingImpact: Judgment is not the end of Hosea's theology; the historical horizon of destruction opens up space for reading the final hope of the book.

investigation: Tyndale's introduction suggests, but does not prove independently, that the final compilation may have occurred in Judah after 722 BC; this should be treated as an editorial hypothesis, not as a safe date.

Matthew Henry conveys ancient traditions about the origin of Hosea (Bet-Semes, tribe of Issachar) and about the long duration of his ministry; the material is traditional and not confirmed by Tyndale's notes.
The order and final form of the book are dealt with widely; the notes affirm a approximately chronological arrangement in 4-14, but do not detail the entire editorial history.
The reading of Gomer as a cultual prostitute, common whore or woman predisposed to adultery remains explicitly debated in the note, so none of these options should be absolutized.

The sources provided mainly cover introduction, chapter 1, chapter 7 and chapter 14; there are no notes attached to various central chapters, so the dossier needs to remain selective and not extrapolate themes without support.

Matthew Henry includes broader literary observations on the conciseness and the sitting character of Hosea, but the coverage here was limited to the attached notes, without reconstructing a full commentary of the book.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends only on the notes provided by Tyndale and Matthew Henry, so the coverage is selective: there are many important elements of Hosea that do not appear in the attached sources and therefore were not included. Where Tyndale's introduction offers historical reconstructions, they were treated as statements of the secondary source, not as independent evidence. The traditions cited by Matthew Henry about origin, tribal affiliation, and the collection of the minor prophets are mentioned as ancient tradition, not as right data. There are also explicit controversies about the type of prostitution in Os 1:2, and the dossier records the debate without closing the issue. Finally, the chronology used here follows only the milestones explicitly cited in the notes; no exact dates have been added beyond those that the source itself presents or presupposes.
